title: 50 Things You Don’t Have To Do For Effective Classroom Management -classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens by arguing that effective classroom management should feel liberating rather than exhausting, since it is knowledge-based rather than effort-based. The bulk of the article is a numbered list of 50 stressful or ineffective methods teachers commonly believe are necessary — lecturing, yelling, micromanaging, bribery, walking on eggshells, giving false praise, tolerating disrespect, and dozens more — framed as things that can be entirely discarded once proven strategies replace them. He closes by directing readers to the archives of the website to learn the actual principles that make these burdensome habits unnecessary, promising that consistent, patient application will lead to dramatically reduced stress and improved results.
points: Effective classroom management is framed as knowledge-based rather than effort-based; if it feels exhausting, something is being done wrong.
The 50-item list catalogs common but ineffective teacher behaviors, including yelling, micromanaging, bribery, false praise, and tolerating disrespect.
Behavior contracts, over-the-top praise, and inconsistent standards for different students are specifically named as unnecessary and counterproductive.
The article positions all 50 items as myths or misconceptions that can be replaced by proven, low-effort strategies detailed elsewhere on the site.
Linsin frames the payoff of dropping these habits as a dramatic reduction in teacher stress alongside improved student behavior.
quotes: You see, exceptional classroom management is knowledge based, not effort based.
Done right, classroom management should feel liberating. In large part, this feeling of liberation comes from what you don’t have to do.

To completely and blissfully rid yourself of the above methods, and to create the classroom you’ve always wanted, you must learn the classroom management principles, strategies, and solutions that are proven to work over time.
Look through the archives. Peruse the categories. Take careful notes. And then put what you learn into practice—one simple strategy at a time—until it becomes second nature.
The results will exceed your expectations. Your confidence will soar. And the weight of 50 grand pianos will slide gently off your shoulders.
